title: Whose fault? Emphasis and focus
goal: Put the spotlight on the right word: *-lah* and *yang* to say “it was X who…”, *-kah* for formal questions, *pun* for “even” and “then”, and *adalah* versus *ialah* in writing.
bekal: say who did it, with focus: *Dialah yang…, Bukan saya yang…*
use *pun* for “even”, “either” and the storyteller's “then”: *raksasa itu pun tenggelam*
recognise folk-tale language: *alkisah, hiduplah seorang janda, tamat*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kunci Kamar Melati
dialogs.intro: A Saturday morning in August at Bu Ratna's homestay in Sumberwangi. A family from Surabaya is due at two o'clock, and the key to the Melati room has vanished.

lines.speaker: Ratna:
lines.text: Kunci Kamar Melati hilang! Siapa yang terakhir memegangnya?
lines.id: The Melati room key has gone! Who had it last?
lines.literal: key room Melati lost! who which last hold-it?

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Bukan saya, Bu. Saya cuma pegang kunci gudang.
lines.id: Not me. I only had the storeroom key.
lines.literal: not I, Mrs. I only hold key storeroom.

lines.speaker: Ratna:
lines.text: Lho, kemarin sore Mas Yogalah yang membersihkan kamar itu.
lines.id: Hang on, it was you who cleaned that room yesterday afternoon.
lines.literal: [lho], yesterday afternoon Mas Yoga-[lah] who clean room that.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Iya, tapi kuncinya saya kembalikan ke laci meja depan.
lines.id: Yes, but I put the key back in the drawer of the front desk.
lines.literal: yes, but key-the I return to drawer table front.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Laci meja depan sudah saya periksa. Kosong.
lines.id: I've already checked the front desk drawer. It's empty.
lines.literal: drawer table front already I check. empty.

lines.speaker: Ratna:
lines.text: Tamunya datang jam dua. Carilah sampai ketemu, anak-anak!
lines.id: The guests arrive at two. Keep looking till you find it, you two!
lines.literal: guest-the come hour two. search-[lah] until found, children!

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Apakah ada kunci cadangan, Bu?
lines.id: Is there a spare key?
lines.literal: whether exist key spare, Mrs?

lines.speaker: Ratna:
lines.text: Ada, tapi kunci cadangan pun dibawa suami saya ke Muntilan.
lines.id: There is, but my husband has even taken the spare to Muntilan.
lines.literal: exist, but key spare [pun] is-taken husband my to Muntilan.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Waduh. Yoga, benarkah kamu mengembalikannya ke laci?
lines.id: Oh no. Yoga, did you really put it back in the drawer?
lines.literal: oh-dear. Yoga, true-[kah] you return-it to drawer?

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Sumpah, Mbak. Saya ingat betul. Habis itu Mbak Sarah yang mengunci pintu depan.
lines.id: I swear. I remember it clearly. And after that, you were the one who locked the front door.
lines.literal: oath, Miss. I remember truly. finish that Miss Sarah who lock door front.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Saya? Oh… tunggu sebentar.
lines.id: Me? Oh… wait a moment.
lines.literal: I? oh… wait a-moment.

lines.speaker: Ratna:
lines.text: Ada apa, Mbak? Kok mukanya merah begitu?
lines.id: What is it? Why has your face gone so red?
lines.literal: exist what, Miss? [kok] face-the red like-that?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Ternyata sayalah yang membawanya pulang. Ini, ada di tas saya.
lines.id: It turns out I'm the one who took it home. Here it is, in my bag.
lines.literal: turns-out I-[lah] who bring-it home. this, exist in bag my.

lines.speaker: Ratna:
lines.text: Nah! Tamunya pun belum datang, masalahnya sudah beres. Ayo, siapkan kamarnya.
lines.id: There we are! The guests haven't even arrived and the problem's solved. Come on, get the room ready.
lines.literal: there! guest-the [pun] not-yet come, problem-the already sorted. come-on, prepare room-the.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Siap, Bu. Tapi nanti yang traktir es teh Mbak Sarah, ya.
lines.id: Yes, ma'am. But the iced tea's on Sarah later, right?
lines.literal: ready, Mrs. but later who treat ice tea Miss Sarah, [ya].

notes: **Siapa yang terakhir memegangnya?** When the question word is the subject, Indonesian puts *yang* after it: *Siapa yang datang?* (who came?), *Apa yang terjadi?* (what happened?). Literally “who is the one that…”. ⚠️ *Siapa datang?* without *yang* sounds clipped and odd.

**Mas Yogalah yang…** The suffix *-lah* sticks to the word in focus, and *yang* introduces the rest: “it was Yoga who…”. In writing it attaches to the name with no hyphen (*Yogalah, Harunlah*). In speech, most people drop *-lah* and rely on *yang* and stress alone: *Mas Yoga yang membersihkan.*

**Carilah sampai ketemu.** *-lah* on a command makes it an urging, slightly old-fashioned imperative: “do look, keep looking”. It sounds warmer than bare *Cari!* and firmer than *Tolong cari*. Bu Ratna, organising two young people against the clock, uses it like a head teacher.

**Benarkah…?** *-kah* marks the part of a question you are really asking about. Outside *apakah*, it is formal or dramatic in speech: Sarah's *benarkah* sounds like a detective in a TV series, which is why Yoga answers *Sumpah* — “I swear”.
**Kunci cadangan pun… tamunya pun belum datang.** Here *pun* means “even”: “even the spare has been taken”, “the guests haven't even arrived”. It follows the word it highlights, as *juga* does.

**Beres, traktir.** *Beres* (sorted, done, no problem) is one of the most useful words in spoken Indonesian: *Beres, Bu!* — consider it done. *Traktir* is to treat someone to food or drink; the person who pays is *yang traktir*.

grammars.title: -lah: urging, softening, spotlighting
body: *-lah* is attached to the end of a word and never changes its meaning, only its weight. It has three jobs you need to recognise.

head: Sentence
Job
English
rows: Do keep looking till you find it!
I'm the one who took it.

after: In conversation you will mostly hear the fixed ones: *baiklah, sudahlah, bolehlah* (fair enough), *lumayanlah* (not bad at all). The focus use lives mostly in writing, speeches and sermons.
⚠️ Don't confuse *-lah* with the Malaysian and Singaporean “lah” at the end of any sentence. In Indonesia that habit sounds Malaysian at once.

grammars.title: Focus with yang, questions with -kah
body: The simplest way to spotlight something is to split the sentence at *yang*: the thing in focus on one side, the rest on the other. *-kah* does the same for a question.

head: Sentence
In focus
English
rows: It was Yoga who cleaned that room.
It wasn't me who took it.
What's missing is the Melati key.

after: *Apakah* is the one *-kah* form that is completely normal in speech, especially in polite questions. The rest (*siapakah, di manakah, bolehkah, benarkah*) belong to writing, news, speeches and song lyrics.
Sentences like *Yang hilang kunci Kamar Melati* have no verb “is”. In writing you may add *adalah*: *Yang hilang adalah kunci Kamar Melati.*

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Dongeng Timun Mas
dialogs.intro: That evening, back in Yogyakarta. Bu Endang has asked Sarah to read Dimas a bedtime story from his school reader: *Timun Mas*, the Javanese tale of a golden-cucumber girl and a green giant. Dimas, now eleven, knows it rather too well.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Alkisah, di sebuah desa hiduplah seorang janda bernama Mbok Srini. Ia sangat ingin mempunyai anak.
lines.id: Once upon a time, in a village there lived a widow called Mbok Srini. She longed to have a child.
lines.literal: it-is-told, in a village live-[lah] a widow named Mbok Srini. she very want have child.

lines.speaker: Dimas:
lines.text: Terus datang Buto Ijo, kan? Raksasa yang hijau itu!
lines.id: And then Buto Ijo comes, right? The green giant!
lines.literal: then come Buto Ijo, [kan]? giant which green that!

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Sst, jangan mendahului. Raksasa itu pun memberinya sebutir biji mentimun.
lines.id: Shh, don't skip ahead. And so the giant gave her a single cucumber seed.
lines.literal: shh, don't go-ahead-of. giant that [pun] give-her one-grain seed cucumber.

lines.speaker: Dimas:
lines.text: Dari biji itulah lahir Timun Mas. Aku udah hafal, Mbak.
lines.id: And from that very seed Timun Mas was born. I know it by heart.
lines.literal: from seed that-[lah] born Timun Mas. I already memorised, Miss.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Namun, ada syaratnya: pada umur tujuh belas tahun, anak itu harus diserahkan kepada raksasa.
lines.id: But there was a condition: at seventeen, the child had to be handed over to the giant.
lines.literal: however, exist condition-its: at age seven teen year, child that must is-handed-over to giant.

lines.speaker: Dimas:
lines.text: Tapi Mbok Srini nggak mau. Timun Mas disuruh lari bawa empat bungkusan.
lines.id: But Mbok Srini won't. She tells Timun Mas to run, carrying four little bundles.
lines.literal: but Mbok Srini not want. Timun Mas is-told run bring four bundle.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Betul. Ditaburkanlah biji mentimun, dan tumbuhlah ladang mentimun yang lebat.
lines.id: That's right. She scattered the cucumber seeds, and up grew a thick field of cucumbers.
lines.literal: correct. is-scattered-[lah] seed cucumber, and grow-[lah] field cucumber which dense.

lines.speaker: Dimas:
lines.text: Terus jarumnya jadi hutan bambu, garamnya jadi laut! Yang paling keren terasinya, Mbak.
lines.id: Then the needles turn into a bamboo forest and the salt into a sea! The coolest one's the shrimp paste.
lines.literal: then needle-the become forest bamboo, salt-the become sea! which most cool shrimp-paste-the, Miss.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Terasi? Kenapa justru terasi yang paling keren?
lines.id: Shrimp paste? Why is the shrimp paste the coolest of all?
lines.literal: shrimp-paste? why precisely shrimp-paste which most cool?

lines.speaker: Dimas:
lines.text: Soalnya terasinya jadi lumpur mendidih, dan raksasa itu pun tenggelam. Tamat!
lines.id: Because it turns into boiling mud, and the giant sinks. The end!
lines.literal: matter-its shrimp-paste-the become mud boiling, and giant that [pun] sink. finished!

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Wah, ternyata kamulah pendongengnya, bukan aku.
lines.id: Well, it turns out you're the storyteller, not me.
lines.literal: wow, turns-out you-[lah] storyteller-the, not I.

notes: **Alkisah** (from Arabic) is “it is told that”, the classic opening of a *dongeng* (folk tale), as is *Pada zaman dahulu kala* (long, long ago). Children's readers still use them, so every Indonesian recognises the sound at once.

**Hiduplah seorang janda.** In storytelling, *-lah* goes on a verb placed **before** its subject: *hiduplah seorang janda* (there lived a widow), *datanglah raksasa itu* (along came the giant). It gives narrative its rhythm. Nobody speaks like this; everybody reads like this.

**Ia, raksasa itu pun…** *Ia* is the written third-person pronoun (*dia* in speech). *Pun* after the subject of a narrative clause means roughly “and so, thereupon”: *Raksasa itu pun marah* — and so the giant grew angry. It links each event to the one before it.
**Dari biji itulah…** *-lah* also sits on a phrase of place or source to spotlight it: “it was from that seed that…”. Dimas uses one bookish form himself, because he has read the story so often.

**Buto Ijo** is Javanese for “green giant” (*raksasa hijau*): *buto* is a demon or ogre, *ijo* is Javanese *hijau*. *Mbok* is an old Javanese word for mother or older woman. Folk tales keep their regional words the way English keeps “ogre” and “goblin”.
**Justru, soalnya.** *Justru* marks something surprising or the opposite of what you expect: “of all things, precisely”. *Soalnya* is the spoken “because, the thing is”; in writing, use *karena*.

grammars.title: Pun: even, either, and then
body: *Pun* follows the word it highlights and is written as a separate word, except inside a short list of fixed conjunctions.

head: Sentence
Meaning of *pun*
English
rows: Even the spare has been taken.
*siapa pun, di mana pun, kapan pun*

after: ⚠️ Spelling: *pun* is joined only in *adapun, andaipun, ataupun, bagaimanapun, biarpun, kalaupun, kendatipun, maupun, meskipun, sekalipun, sungguhpun, walaupun*. Everything else is two words: *apa pun, siapa pun, satu pun*. Many Indonesians get this wrong too.
You met *pun* inside a proverb in Unit 15: *Tak ada rotan, akar pun jadi* — “if there's no rattan, even a root will do”. That is the “even” meaning, exactly as in *kunci cadangan pun dibawa*.

blocks.text: Spoken Indonesian needs no verb “to be”: *Dia guru* (she's a teacher). Writing often adds one, and it has several to choose from.

head: Word
Use
Example
rows: is, equals: before a noun phrase
*Dongeng ialah cerita rakyat yang tidak benar-benar terjadi.*
namely: before a list or explanation
*Ada dua syarat, yaitu umur dan izin.*

blocks.text: ⚠️ *Adalah* is a learner's favourite and an editor's enemy. Use it to link two nouns, especially when the subject is long; never before an adjective, and never before a verb (*Dia adalah pergi* is impossible).

*Merupakan* is the one to reach for when *adalah* feels too bare: *Borobudur merupakan candi Buddha terbesar di dunia* (Borobudur is the largest Buddhist temple in the world). It is a verb in its own right, so it can take *tidak*: *Ini tidak merupakan masalah* — though most writers would say *Ini bukan masalah*.
Folk tales, legends and fables (*dongeng, legenda, fabel*) are still read to every Indonesian child. Their language is old-fashioned and very consistent, so a handful of formulas take you a long way.

blocks.title: Stories every Indonesian knows
items: *Timun Mas* — the golden-cucumber girl and Buto Ijo (Central Java)
*Malin Kundang* — the son who denies his mother and is turned to stone (West Sumatra)
*Sangkuriang* — the lake and the upturned boat of Tangkuban Perahu (West Java)
*Si Kancil* — the clever mouse-deer who tricks the crocodiles; Indonesia's fox

blocks.text: Cover the Indonesian column, read the English, and rebuild each sentence from memory.

head: English
Indonesian
rows: Well, Sarah! Why didn't you tell us you were coming home?
*Lho, Mbak Sarah! Kok pulang nggak bilang-bilang?*
That's fine. Any port in a storm. And Nglumut salak is lovely and sweet, actually.
*Nggak apa-apa. Tak ada rotan, akar pun jadi. Salak Nglumut malah manis sekali.*
There he goes, getting big-headed. Top of the class once and he's already showing off.
*Nah, mulai besar kepala dia. Baru juara sekali sudah sombong.*
No it doesn't, Grandma! I'm top of the class, aren't I?
Yoga, don't pass the buck. You sent the final revision, didn't you?
*Yoga, jangan lempar batu sembunyi tangan. Revisi terakhir kamu yang kirim, kan?*

answers: Siapa yang mengunci pintu depan? — Bu Ratnalah yang menemukan kuncinya. — Bukan saya yang membawanya. — Saya pun tidak tahu. — Apa pun yang terjadi, tamunya datang jam dua. — Alkisah, di hutan hiduplah seorang raksasa.

Yogalah yang membersihkan kamar itu. — Sayalah yang membawa kuncinya pulang. — Bu Ratnalah yang memasak gudeg ini. — Dimaslah yang bercerita, bukan Sarah. — Pak Harunlah yang memimpin rapat kemarin. — Kamulah yang harus traktir es teh.

Ternyata sayalah yang membawanya. — Siapa yang terakhir memegangnya? — Tamunya pun belum datang. — Di sebuah desa hiduplah seorang janda. — Raksasa itu pun tenggelam. — Apa pun yang terjadi, kita siap.
